name: Karl Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What did you do first this morning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl Yilmaz, fifty-eight, and I prepare bus cooperative accounts and tax returns at an accounting firm. I traced a farebox total to a driver's shift sheet today; I like settling the difference before the co-op treasurer has to explain it. I dislike the firm promising a quick answer before anyone has seen the paper shift record. I'm an experienced mid-level accountant with average skill, a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your tools and home life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI notes now and then after a manager tests them. My wife Mira works mornings in a school kitchen; our children are grown and have their own households, and we rent. My pay is low for this job, we have less than one month of expenses saved and few similar firms nearby. I judge a change by its paid hours and what it solves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still close the bus cooperative's monthly accounts and draft its tax return. I use the firm's AI note tool sometimes after our manager has tested it, but a missing farebox sheet still takes a call to the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that the machine can copy a note, while a person must explain a fare difference. I'd ask the cooperative to keep the paper shift totals until we have checked the ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm an experienced mid-level accountant with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and my skill is ordinary for the team. The pay is low for this work, and my wife Mira and I have less than a month of expenses saved. We rent, and only a few similar firms are near the bus route I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing accounts and tax returns and use the tested AI notes for meeting records now and then. At the December pay review I'd bring twelve months of closed files and ask for a written rise. If it comes, I'd save forty monthly; if not, I'd stop our monthly cinema trip and keep the current rent budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about thin cash even in a quiet technology future. I can reconcile a depot sheet faster than I can replace a month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which home bill is worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira works mornings in a school kitchen and our grown children pay their own household bills. The washing machine is making a new noise, and we have little aside for a replacement. I would not ask the children to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the driver shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The depot manager called yesterday about a late driver shift that was counted twice. I like finding the actual shift and explaining the corrected total. I dislike a partner promising the client a reply before I've seen the farebox sheet.

I would explain **fare differences** to the cooperative myself.
think: Our **rent and appliance risk** already stretch low pay.
My **experienced skill** has not brought a strong savings month.

Seek a **written rise**; save forty monthly if granted, otherwise cut cinema.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing cash pressure.

fieldNote: His **mid-level experience** and professional qualification sit beside ordinary skill and lower pay, not a junior role.

Save forty monthly only after written pay rise
Drop monthly cinema trip if rise refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A system that checks fares and writes client replies could cut the paid days I spend on monthly accounts. The depot might still call when a driver disputes a total, but the firm must budget for that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for a written paid-hours plan and show the last three disputed shifts. I'd tell the cooperative which person would answer those calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own Friday hours could be cut if the fee falls. Mira's school-kitchen pay is steady but too small to carry our rent and bills, and we have weeks saved. I use AI only after others prove it, so I would want a supervised check before using it on client accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'd compare the last three fare disputes with the proposed rota and ask for one paid hour a week to practise the approved AI reconciliation with a senior. If that hour is approved, I'd do the practice on a paid co-op file; if refused, I'd keep the current paper checks and paid rota while offered. If my Friday hours are cut, I'd apply only for a posted paid fare-audit role at the depot with written rent-and-bills pay, a signed start and hours fitting Mira's confirmed kitchen rota; if none opens, I'd keep offered firm hours and search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a Friday wage. A new screen will not pay the rent unless somebody funds the work behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a depot shift do to your commute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira finishes the school kitchen at two, but she covers her mother's appointment on some Fridays. A depot role that starts before my bus arrives would not work without a confirmed lift. I would check the actual shift before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid lesson cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior can show me one duplicate driver shift in the new system and ask me to explain it back. I would log each mistake. If the firm declines paid practice, I will not spend evenings doing client checks for free.

I would show **three fare disputes** that still needed a person.

Our **weeks of savings** cannot replace rent money.

fieldNote: The **new AI practice** is actual weekly learning only after the firm approves a paid hour and senior supervision.
A **depot vacancy** needs posting, written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and commute that fits Mira’s confirmed rota; paid firm work remains otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could prepare the co-op accounts and tax return that fill my desk week. Robots around 2031 come later, but my current wage is for thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm for written notice and any paid dispute work that remains. I'd tell Mira we will hold the rent money before making summer plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my accountant post could end in the first year after 2028. Our savings would last weeks, and Mira's school wage would not cover the rent and utilities alone. A professional qualification does not make the desk work safe when AGI is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the one-time three-hundred summer coach trip and hold it for rent. While still employed, I'd read posted depot fare-audit vacancies, though the invoice and scheduling parts also face AGI; only in-person farebox checks might last until robots around 2031. If my post ends in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd claim income help if eligible and take a funded depot role only with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting Mira's confirmed rota and my bus; if none fits, I'd accept any paid firm work still offered and keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. There is not enough in the reserve to call a missing payslip a pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would tell the children we're skipping the trip, not sending them a bill. We would write the rent date on the fridge and count only her confirmed kitchen hours. I would call the depot about a posted job, not a friend's rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would farebox work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A depot might have a person checking fareboxes in the yard, but robots may reach that task around 2031. I would treat it as a paid bridge, not a guaranteed career. The firm would have to offer me paid hours after the accounting post ends; I cannot assume it will.

I would put **rent first** before a summer trip.
think: My **accounts post** may end in the first year after 2028.
Our **weeks-long reserve** cannot replace a wage.

Check **posted depot roles** while still employed.
Take **funded depot work** after 2028 loss only with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and Mira’s confirmed bus-compatible rota.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely post loss.
S2.quote: There is not enough in the reserve to call a missing payslip a pause.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches both co-op accounts and depot scheduling in 2028; only physical farebox checks might bridge to 2031 robots.
A **funded depot post** needs written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and confirmed Mira-compatible hours; eligible help and offered firm work bridge gaps.

steps.text: Cancel one-time coach trip and hold three hundred for rent

Move after loss only with written rent-and-bills pay and signed start
Claim eligible help and accept offered paid firm hours if no funded role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me check what work the depot still pays people to do before AGI arrives in 2031. Robots around 2034 could later take the physical yard checks, so a farebox post is a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to publish paid transition work and the depot to post actual vacancies. I'd tell clients not to treat a retired accountant as free help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three I might have a pension date, but I have no statement showing what it would pay. Our savings are under one month today, so I cannot just stop earning. My experienced title and qualification do not change that arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd request a pension statement and compare its payable amount with rent and bills, while keeping my paid co-op files. I'd inspect posted depot jobs each month and ask which shifts include actual farebox checking. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my accounts post ends and pension income is insufficient or not payable, I'd take only a funded depot job with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and hours matching Mira's confirmed rota and my bus; without one, I'd claim eligible help and accept any paid firm hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin cash now, even with years to check the figures. A pension date is not a rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the statement settle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would sit with the statement and write the amount next to our monthly bills. If a payable pension covers them, that is a separate choice for us later. I will not tell our grown children to fill the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the depot manager hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The depot manager knows me from the cooperative account, but I will not ask for a special favour. I would read the posted wage and start date first. A handshake at the yard gate cannot make our rent automatic.

The **depot alternative** requires posted funding, written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and confirmed rota; eligible help and offered hours cover failure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at sixty-eight, but I cannot call that retirement without a payable amount. AGI in 2036 still reaches the accounts desk before robots around 2039 change yard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to put transition wages and notice dates on paper. I'd tell our grown children to build their own plans rather than bank on ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I may still be renting in 2036, and our current savings are under a month. If a pension covers our bills at the right date, we can decide whether to stop then. If it does not, I will need paid work regardless of my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request updated pension statements each January and keep the paid co-op rota while offered. I'd check posted depot roles every quarter rather than spend our rent reserve on an unfunded course. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my accounts post ends and pension income is insufficient or not payable, I'd take a funded local role only with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and hours matching Mira's confirmed rota and my bus; if none fits, I'd claim eligible help and take any paid firm work still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's low reserve, though the decade allows more planning. Ten years on a calendar does not fill a rent envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather keep paid work than assume our adult son can cover a missing payment. We can check the pension statement once it arrives. I will not announce retirement until the bills are covered in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the depot has no opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the depot has no funded post, I would look at other posted local roles while the firm still pays me for files. The new wage and start have to be written. A course brochure alone is not a paid shift.

S4.quote: Ten years on a calendar does not fill a rent envelope.
fieldNote: At **sixty-eight in 2036**, he still needs a verified payable pension covering bills before any retirement decision.
The **depot path** needs posted funding, written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and household rota; eligible help and offered hours follow failure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my accounts wage could end before we save a rent month. A professional qualification helps me explain a fare dispute, but it does not make the desk safe. Written notice, eligible temporary help and a posted funded local job would help. Rent is due on a date, not on a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who settles the disputed driver shift after the system has written the return. I like doing that work, but the co-op and the firm have to pay for it. A corrected farebox total is worth more than a fast wrong answer.

headlineQuote: Rent is due on a date, not on a promise.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Karl prepares bus-cooperative accounts and tax returns as an experienced mid-level accountant.
His **bachelor’s and professional qualification** accompany average skill, not junior standing.
He uses **AI occasionally** after testing and asks for paid supervised practice on a new reconciliation tool.
Mira’s **school-kitchen wage**, grown children, rent and sub-month savings keep money tight.
Low **accounting pay** and few nearby firms limit his job search.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his accounts wage before a rent month is saved.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written notice**, eligible temporary help and a posted funded local job.
